Caul of the Liver
KAWL of the LIV-er
noun
Caul is from the Old French cale, a covering or membrane, rendering the Hebrew yothereth, an appendage or lobe. It names the fatty membrane or lobe upon the liver, burnt with the fat upon the altar; not the women’s netted headdress of Isaiah 3.

Biblical Definition

The caul of the liver was the fatty membrane or lobe lying above the liver, singled out by the LORD to be taken with the fat and the kidneys and burnt upon the altar in every offering. At Aaron’s consecration it is named: “the caul that is above the liver, and the two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them” (Exo 29:13). It recurs through the law of sacrifice — in the peace offering, “the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away” (Lev 3:4, 3:10) — and in the sin offering Aaron “burnt upon the altar” the fat, the kidneys, and the caul above the liver (Lev 9:10). These innermost and richest parts, hidden deep within the beast, were the LORD’s portion, reserved wholly for Him and consumed in the fire of the altar. Herein is a searching lesson. God claimed not merely the outward flesh but the inward fat, the choicest and most secret part; He would have the best, and He would have the inmost. So He requires of His people not the surface of religion but the hidden man of the heart, the inward parts given up to Him. What the caul figured in the beast, the whole devotion of the soul must render in the worshipper: the deepest and richest of us laid upon the altar and offered up to God.

Webster 1828 Definition

The fatty membrane or lobe above the liver, taken with the fat and burnt upon the altar in the offerings.

expand to see more

CAUL OF THE LIVER, the fatty membrane or lobe lying upon the liver of a sacrificial beast.

It was taken away with the fat and the two kidneys and burnt upon the altar.

It is named in the consecration offering and throughout the law of the offerings.

The Hebrew doctors take it for the midriff or the lobe appended to the liver.

It is distinct from the caul as a woman’s netted headdress named in Isaiah’s reproof.

Key Scripture

Exo 29:13 — "And thou shalt take all the fat that covereth the inwards, and the caul that is above the liver, and the two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them, and burn them upon the altar."

Lev 3:4 — "And the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away."

Lev 3:10 — "And the two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away."

Lev 9:10 — "But the fat, and the kidneys, and the caul above the liver of the sin offering, he burnt upon the altar; as the LORD commanded Moses."

Modern Corruption

A part of the offering, not a contested doctrine; it recovers God’s claim upon the inmost and best of the worshipper.

expand to see more

The caul of the liver rebukes a religion of the surface that gives God the outward flesh and keeps back the hidden fat. The age offers Him its spare hours and its public shows, but reserves the inmost heart for itself. The law that claimed the caul and the kidneys — the deepest and richest parts — testifies that God will not be served with the outside only, but requires the secret man within.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD claims the inmost and the best. The fat and the caul, hidden deep within the beast, were burnt wholly to Him; so He asks of us the hidden man of the heart, the choicest of our love laid upon the altar. It is distinct from the cauls, the women’s headdress of Isaiah’s day.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The fatty lobe above the liver, the LORD’s inward portion in the offering, figuring the surrender of the inmost heart.

expand to see more

Caul of the liver — the fatty membrane above the liver, burnt with the fat and kidneys (Exo 29:13).

It recurs through the law of the peace and sin offerings (Lev 3:4; Lev 9:10).

The word caul is from Old French cale, a covering or membrane.

These innermost, richest parts were reserved wholly as the LORD’s portion.

It is distinct from cauls, the netted headdress of the women of Isaiah 3.

Usage

"The caul above the liver was the LORD’s, burnt upon the altar with the fat."

"God claimed not the outward flesh only but the inmost and richest part."

"As the caul was given whole to God, so must the hidden heart be laid upon the altar."
